title: What is known about 1RB0LA_0LC0RA_1LA1LD_1LC0LE_1RF0LF_0RB---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LA_0LC0RA_1LA1LD_1LC0LE_1RF0LF_0RB---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is a sequence of domains, each a periodic pattern (mostly built from 10, 0111 and blocks of 1s), separated by walls that barely move. At the left end a block of 1s grows by about two cells per visit of the head until it is frozen into a domain of 10s, and a new block starts. The right end grows by one cell at rare events (62 in 3·109 steps). No macro map is known.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: If the machine halts on its third step from a configuration, that configuration is one of: D with 1 two left, 1 left, 1 under the head. So a run can reach a halt only through one of these patterns, and a proof that the machine never halts only has to rule them out. The proof splits on the state and the five cells around the head.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 49,910 cells have been visited and 35,869 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Sweeps over 10s
claims.text: B crosses (10)^n to the right in 2n steps, turning it into (01)^n; C crosses it to the left with a 1 ahead in 2n steps, turning it into ones.

claims.title: Rare events at the right end
claims.text: Up to 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps the right end grows 62 times (at 9176, 13365, 18394, …, 2173474752, 2810209489), and its position moves from 42 to 70 cells right of the start between 7.6·10<sup>6</sup> and 1.9·10<sup>9</sup> steps.

claims.title: Domains with frozen walls
claims.text: In the defect picture (period 4) the tape is cut into regions by vertical, i.e. stationary, walls; new regions are born at the left end with lengths that grow from one to the next.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.512). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.09).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Next step: Find what freezes the left block (a signal from the right end?), the sequence of block lengths, and the rewriting rules of the domains; then accelerate by domain events.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine builds its tape out of domains, stretches of different repeating patterns with walls that barely move. A block of ones grows at one end and is frozen into a new domain again and again.

facts.text: How the head crosses domains of 10s, proved for every length.
Growth steps of the slow right end in 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps.
No halt in the C simulator; 49,910 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: Domains and walls
html:
The tape is made of stretches of different repeating patterns (domains) separated by walls that stay in place. At the left end, a block of 1s grows by about two cells per visit of the head; at some moment the whole block is turned into a domain of 10s (the grey wedges) and a new block starts. The domains are then rewritten by later sweeps into other patterns (dark), while their walls stay put. The right end grows by one cell at rare events.

A halt needs F reading 1; no candidate configuration has been seen. What triggers the freezing of the block, and what the domains encode, is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.512). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.09).
After 109 steps the tape spans 49,910 cells (36,650 left of the start, 65 right), with a density of 1s of 0.719.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

family: Domain builder: a block of ones at the fast end frozen into ever longer domains
summary: A block of ones grows at the left end and is periodically frozen into a new domain of 10s; the tape is a growing list of periodic domains with stationary walls, and the slow right end grows by one cell at rare events; halting needs F reading 1.
